overview: The Bosporan kingdom joined Greek cities and neighbouring communities around the Kerch Strait, between Crimea and the Taman Peninsula. Its ports connected grain-growing country with the wider Greek world. The map shows only 323 to 1 BCE within a much longer history, and its broad northern outline should not be read as continuous royal control over every place inside it.

periods.title: Hellenistic centuries around the strait
periods.summary: Spartocid rulers and their successors governed a kingdom whose cities faced one another across the water.

items.text: Bosporan rulers used different titles for different subjects: archon, or chief magistrate, of Greek cities such as Bosporus and Theodosia, but king of peoples including the Sindi. Panticapaeum and Phanagoria were important centres on opposite sides of the strait. One royal court dealt with communities that had different political traditions.

In 285/4 BCE Athens honoured King Spartokos III after his gift of 15,000 medimnoi of grain. A medimnos was a measure of dry produce. The decree turns a shipload-sized problem, feeding a city, into a surviving written record of international friendship.

The Athenians voted a gold crown and bronze statues for Spartokos. The surviving decree names an Agora location and a second, less securely reconstructed setting. Food supplies could win a ruler a very public thank-you, even far from his own kingdom.

At Phanagoria, fourth-century BCE remains include paved streets, wells, water pipes and rectangular houses with tiled roofs. This neighbourhood evidence begins before the map window. Fetching water and keeping a roof over the family were part of city life alongside the impressive temples.

Builders commonly put mudbrick walls on stone foundations during Phanagoria’s Greek and Roman periods. Later residents reused older building stone, which helps explain why archaeologists often recover only fragments of a house plan. An ancient wall could end up doing a second shift in somebody else’s building.

A gymnasium is reported at Phanagoria from the third century BCE, adding a place for physical training to the city’s public buildings. The surviving foundations tell us about organised activity; they do not provide a class register showing which children could participate.

Imported pottery reached Phanagoria from centres including Athens, Chios and Thasos, while local potters also made vessels inspired by Greek models. A household’s pots could therefore connect local craftwork with distant workshops and sea routes.

A wooden vessel found underwater at Phanagoria in 2012 preserves a rare piece of working maritime technology. Radiocarbon analysis places its wood in the middle of the first century BCE; a bronze bow fitting bears symbols associated with Mithridates VI. Researchers connect the ship with his military fleet.

Scientific examination found clay mixed with animal hair and feathers on the inside of the hull, over tarred fibres in the seams. Outside was a mixture containing wax, conifer resin and the mineral realgar. Researchers interpret these coatings as protection against water, fire and marine organisms. The ship had a surprisingly complicated coat.

sections.title: Words that came back from the sea

items.text: A marble monument from Phanagoria addresses Hypsikrateia, companion of the first-century BCE king Mithridates VI, using the name Hypsikrates. Its last word, in a modern transcription of the ancient Greek, is χαῖρε, meaning “farewell” in this funerary setting. The inscription identifies her as the king’s wife; it does not establish exactly how she died.

The same inscription preserves a small human correction: the stonecutter first wrote one grammatical form of “woman” or “wife”, then changed it to the form needed when addressing her. Even a solemn stone monument could need proofreading.

Later harbour builders reused inscribed stones as construction material. Underwater excavation recovered royal dedications and civic records from that reused stonework. Recycling helped scramble their original settings, but also preserved messages that can now be studied.

The kingdom continued into the Roman imperial period. A Phanagorian inscription honours Aspurgus, a king recognised by Rome in 14 CE. Another records a portico restored in 220 CE after war damage. These are later chapters of Bosporan history, not evidence that the kingdom stopped when this map record does.

ending.text: The map’s 1 BCE endpoint is not the kingdom’s fall. Bosporan royal institutions persisted into late antiquity, and the end of royal coin production does not by itself date the end of government. During the early sixth century CE, imperial intervention brought Bosporus under Byzantine rule. Different cities experienced these changes on different schedules.
